2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate concern / Can't tell: Of 66 women eligible for follow-up interviews after cultural consensus screening (from the 304-person parent sample), 32 participated and 34 (51.5%) did not; reasons for non-participation or refusal between stages are not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable (qualitative descriptive/ethnographic design with no quantitative causal effect estimation; contextual influences such as topography, seasonality, and short-term NGO projects are explored thematically).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / perception-based only: Formal water law, municipal mandates, and DINEPA regulatory rules are not examined via primary legal or administrative records; governance arrangements, informal neighbour-to-neighbour pipe networks, fee collection, and padlock/valve restrictions are documented solely through local perceptions and ethnographic accounts.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Interviews (1-3 hours) were conducted in Haitian Kreyol with real-time translation by a local community translator rather than independent bilingual transcription/back-translation, creating potential translation loss and social-desirability bias regarding neighbourhood water disputes; Appendix A (interview script) is blank in the PDF.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Qualitative experiential measurement only: Water access barriers, schedule intermittency, low pipe pressure, perceived contamination (turbidity, odour, flood/saltwater intrusion), and coping behaviours are richly captured via self-report and site visits, without microbiological water testing, flow metering, or reported HWISE scale statistics.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: Thematic findings and divergent community versus source-manager perspectives are thoroughly illustrated with verbatim quotes, though one outlying belief (malicious water spirits) was explicitly excluded from Results, analytic coding procedures are minimally reported, and Figure 2's map graphic and Appendix A's text are missing in the published PDF.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Sampling procedures for the parent 304-woman survey are unreported in this paper; follow-up eligibility was restricted to the top 10% for peer-shared responses on at least two of four unpublished cultural consensus domains (n=66, with 32 interviewed), systematically favouring culturally conformist informants and potentially excluding marginalized perspectives, while recruitment of quoted source managers is undescribed.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The Introduction explicitly enumerates two clear research aims: (1) providing information on the status of water infrastructure in Gressier, Haiti where official records are inaccessible, and (2) exploring women's perceptions of water quality, infrastructure barriers, and community-led solutions to water insecurity, with clear justification of relevance in post-earthquake Haiti.

Qualitative semi-structured interviews and ethnographic site visits are directly appropriate for investigating women's lived experiences, subjective perceptions of water quality and treatment, informal pipe-sharing practices, and social tensions around local water management.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors justify combining in-home semi-structured interviews with ethnographic visits to household water sources, allowing iterative questioning until saturation and organizing findings thematically rather than geographically because water access varied sharply even among immediate neighbours and baseline infrastructure maps were unavailable.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: While the authors explain screening a parent sample of 304 women (>16 years residing in Gressier) down to 66 key informants in the top 10% of shared agreement on at least two of four cultural consensus domains (with 32 agreeing to interviews), they do not describe how the original 304 women were recruited, why 34 of 66 eligible women (51.5%) did not participate, how quoted source managers were recruited, or whether restricting selection to high-consensus peers excluded marginalized or minority water experiences.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection methods are clearly specified: 1-3 hour in-home semi-structured interviews paired with water-source site visits in March-April 2018, conducted in Haitian Kreyol with real-time translation by a trained community translator, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and iteratively adapted as emergent themes arose until saturation was reached (note that Appendix A's script body is omitted/blank on PDF Page 21, though the dynamic questioning approach is explained in text).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the authors briefly note that flexible interviewing was intended to reduce interviewer bias beyond the research team's preconceptions, there is no critical reflexivity regarding how US university researchers' positionality in an aid-dependent Haitian commune or the presence of a translator from the local community shaped participant disclosures, expectations of assistance, or willingness to criticize local water managers.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper states only that interviews were audio-recorded with verbal consent from informants and that women over 16 years old were eligible (including a quoted 16-year-old student). No Institutional Review Board (IRB) or Haitian ethics committee approval is reported anywhere in the article, nor are parental consent/assent procedures for 16-17 year old minors or confidentiality safeguards in close-knit neighbourhoods discussed.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 5-6] Methods (pp. 904-905); [PDF Page 10] Results (p. 909); [PDF Page 18] Acknowledgments/Disclosure/Funding (p. 917)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: Data analysis is described in a single sentence stating that major themes were coded using NVivo software, alongside a note on pursuing saturation and omitting an unsupported outlier belief (malicious water spirits). The paper provides no details on the number of coders, codebook development, inductive versus deductive coding mechanics, inter-coder reliability, or participant validation.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly structured across eight thematic subsections, substantiated with rich contextualized quotes from diverse women and local source managers, explicitly present competing viewpoints (e.g. community suspicion of corruption versus source managers' protective rationale; differing views on pre-chlorination), and directly address the study's aims and international development metrics.

Valuable qualitative contribution (narrative assessment): The study illuminates why standard WHO/MDG 'improved versus unimproved' water metrics fail to capture real-world household water insecurity in peri-urban Haiti, documenting hydraulic pressure collapse from informal neighbour-to-neighbour PVC extensions, post-NGO maintenance and governance vacuums, fee/trust breakdowns, and the potential of local grassroots water committees, while outlining concrete directions for governance and mapping research.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable (clear contribution to WaSH infrastructure governance literature and practice)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This primary qualitative study (semi-structured interviews and ethnographic site visits with 32 women and local water source managers in Gressier, Haiti) demonstrates moderate methodological concern on the CASP Qualitative Checklist (5 'Yes', 1 'No', and 3 'Can't tell' ratings across Q1-Q9, plus high substantive value on Q10). Strengths include clearly articulated aims (Q1), an appropriate qualitative/ethnographic design incorporating water-source site visits and iterative probing to saturation (Q2, Q3, Q5), and rich, nuanced reporting of thematic findings that contrast community member and source-manager perspectives (Q9). Key methodological limitations include the absence of researcher reflexivity regarding foreign academic positionality and local community-translator dynamics (Q6: No); incomplete reporting of recruitment for the parent 304-woman survey, unexplained non-participation by 34 of 66 consensus-screened women, undocumented recruitment of source managers, and potential conformity bias from restricting selection to top-10% cultural-consensus peers (Q4: Can't tell); lack of reported IRB/ethics committee approval or minor-protection protocols despite enrolling participants over age 16 (Q7: Can't tell); and minimal description of the NVivo coding and thematic derivation process (Q8: Can't tell).
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (1 No and 3 Can't tell items out of Q1-Q9)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative study (semi-structured in-home interviews and ethnographic water-source site visits with a purposively screened subsample of 32 women, nested within a larger household water study)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Aims and rationale: [PDF Page 2-3] Abstract & Introduction (pp. 901-902); Study context: [PDF Page 3-5] Study site (pp. 902-904); Sampling, interviews, translation, consent, and NVivo coding: [PDF Page 5-6] Methods (pp. 904-905) and [PDF Page 21] Appendix A header (p. 920, script body omitted in PDF); Thematic findings and participant/manager quotes: [PDF Page 6-15] Results (pp. 905-914); Interpretation, policy critique, future directions, and disclosures: [PDF Page 15-18] Discussion, Conclusions, Acknowledgments, Disclosure, and Funding (pp. 914-917).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Although nested within a broader project that administered the HWISE scale and an unpublished cultural consensus questionnaire to 304 women, no quantitative survey data or mixed-methods integration are reported in this article (the cultural consensus tool was used solely as a purposive screening filter to identify eligible key informants). All empirical data collected, analyzed, and presented here consist of primary qualitative semi-structured interviews and ethnographic observations, making the CASP Qualitative Checklist the exact matching instrument.
